title: Video Stitching
statement:
A sporting event runs from second `0` to second `time`. Each entry `clips[i] = [start_i, end_i]` is a recording of the stretch from `start_i` to `end_i`; recordings may overlap, may have any length (even zero), and may run past `time`. Any chosen clip can be trimmed into as many smaller pieces as you like.

Return the smallest number of clips whose pieces together cover the whole interval `[0, time]` without gaps, or `-1` if no choice of clips covers it.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every subset of clips is exponential. Since clips can be trimmed, the only thing that matters about a set of chosen clips is how far right their union reaches from `0` without a hole. This is the "jump game" in disguise: from each starting second, record the farthest end any clip reaches, then walk left to right and take a new clip only when the current coverage runs out, always choosing the one that reaches farthest.

## Approach

1. Build `reach`, where `reach[s]` is the largest `end` among clips that start at second `s` (ignore clips starting at or after `time`).
2. Walk `t` from `0` to `time - 1`, keeping `farthest`, the largest end of any clip starting at or before `t`.
3. When `t` reaches `covered` (the end of what the chosen clips already cover), a new clip is needed.
4. If `farthest` does not get past `t`, there is a hole at `t`, so return `-1`.
5. Otherwise take the clip that reaches `farthest`: increase `count` and set `covered = farthest`.
6. Return `count` once the walk finishes.

## Example 1, step by step

With `time = 10`, `reach` holds `2` at second 0, `9` at 1, `6` at 4, `9` at 5 and `10` at 8. At `t = 0`, `farthest = 2`, so take `[0,2]`: `count = 1`, `covered = 2`. By `t = 2`, `farthest = 9` (from `[1,9]`), so `count = 2`, `covered = 9`. At `t = 8`, `farthest` becomes `10`; at `t = 9` coverage runs out again, so `count = 3`, `covered = 10`. The walk ends and the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + time): one pass over the clips and one over the seconds.
- Space: O(time) for `reach`.

## Pitfalls

- A zero-length clip such as `[0,0]` covers nothing; the `farthest <= t` test catches it.
- Clips may end after `time`; that is fine, but a clip starting at or after `time` must not index past `reach`.
- Two clips like `[0,2]` and `[3,5]` leave the hole `(2,3)`; touching ends such as `[0,2]`, `[2,5]` are enough.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `reach` | `reach[s]` is the farthest end of a clip starting at second `s` |
| `count` | clips chosen so far |
| `covered` | the chosen clips cover `[0, covered]` |
| `farthest` | farthest end of any clip starting at or before `t` |
| `t` | the second being scanned |

narration.2: reach[s] will hold the farthest end of any clip that starts at second s.
narration.4: A clip starting at or after time cannot help cover [0, time).
narration.5: Keep only the longest clip for each starting second.
narration.8: No clips have been chosen yet.
narration.9: The chosen clips cover [0, covered]; at the start that is just the point 0.
narration.10: farthest tracks the best end reachable by a clip that starts by second t.
narration.11: Scan the seconds from left to right.
narration.12: Any clip starting at t is now usable, so update the best reachable end.
narration.13: Coverage ends exactly here, so another clip is needed to continue.
narration.14: If no usable clip gets past t, there is a hole right after t.
narration.17: Take the clip that reaches farthest.
narration.18: Coverage now extends to that clip's end.
narration.21: Every second up to time is covered; return how many clips it took.
